methodology: Official HKEAA sources were used to confirm the examination year, Paper 4 framework and timetable, but they do not expose all 24 task sheets as searchable official text.
The full topic map was cross-referenced across a speaking-paper archive and two independent candidate-recall compilations. Candidate-recall wording is never labelled official.
Where recall sources conflicted, the conflict is recorded. A known 2.1/2.3 copy-and-paste swap in one source was not propagated.
No official context passage was reproduced. Every PP replacement contains a newly written 150–220 word mock context tied to the scenario and prompts.
important_findings: The corpus contains 24 PP records plus one separate hidden mock for version 1.3.
Set 6.1 has a substantive Part A defect in the current canonical record: two promotion questions duplicate one another and the unwanted-clothing question is missing. The replacement corrects it.

The exact official wording and official order of Part B questions cannot be established from public sources. The eight recalled concepts are retained, normalised and marked low confidence for exact order.
The 8.1–8.3 records have weaker evidence than 1.1–7.3 because only two indexed archives were found and one of those carries the detailed Part B reconstruction.

context.source_line: Original mock website written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: A Champion Comes Back to School
body: Hong Kong fencer Edgar Cheung Ka-long has shown young people that success in sport is built over many years. Behind his Olympic medals are long training sessions, repeated technical practice and the ability to recover after mistakes. His achievements have also increased local interest in fencing, a sport that many students previously knew only from international competitions on television.

A school visit by Cheung could therefore be more than a celebrity appearance. A short demonstration might introduce basic fencing movements, while an interview could explore pressure, motivation, injuries and the choices required to become a full-time athlete. Students with little interest in sport could still learn about goal-setting, resilience and representing Hong Kong on an international stage.

The organising committee would need to plan carefully. Activities should be safe, inclusive and useful for a large audience, rather than limited to a few experienced athletes. Interview questions should encourage thoughtful answers instead of repeating facts already available online. The committee must also decide how to turn a memorable visit into lasting benefits for students after the event has ended.

context.source_line: Original mock online published article written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: When a Photograph Becomes a Public Problem
body: Popular destinations increasingly face conflicts between visitors looking for striking photographs and residents trying to continue their daily lives. At some crowded locations overseas, barriers, warning signs or restricted areas have been introduced after tourists blocked roads, entered private property or gathered for long periods at the same viewpoint. Such measures can protect safety, but they may also make a place feel less welcoming.

Hong Kong has many locations that attract photographers, from harbour promenades and traditional markets to colourful housing estates. Photography can promote the city and help visitors record meaningful experiences. Problems arise, however, when people photograph strangers without permission, interrupt businesses, damage property or create dangerous crowds simply to copy an image seen on social media.

Rules should therefore respond to specific harm rather than ban photography everywhere. Clear signs, marked photo zones and better crowd management may solve some problems, while serious cases could require penalties. The challenge is to protect privacy, safety and neighbourhood life without preventing responsible visitors from enjoying and sharing public places.

context.source_line: Original mock technology website written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: One Screen Cannot Do Every Job
body: Smartphones have become the main digital device for many young people. They are portable, relatively affordable and able to handle communication, banking, entertainment, navigation and quick searches. Improved cameras and mobile applications have made tasks that once required several separate devices possible from one pocket-sized screen. For everyday use, a phone may seem more convenient than a personal computer.

Yet convenience is not the same as suitability. Writing a long report, comparing several sources, editing detailed images or managing a spreadsheet is often easier with a keyboard, a larger display and desktop software. Students who depend only on phones may be able to consume information quickly but find it harder to produce complex work or organise many files.

The future is therefore unlikely to be a simple victory for one device. Phones may replace computers for more routine tasks, while laptops and desktops remain important for study, creative work and professional use. Schools must consider whether students have fair access to suitable equipment and teach them to choose the right tool rather than use the newest one automatically.

context.source_line: This article appeared on a youth / education website:
context.title: One Device for Everything?
body: For many young people, the smartphone is their camera, map, wallet, television and main way of going online. It is cheaper and more portable than a laptop, and most everyday tasks—messaging, shopping, banking and watching videos—can be completed with a few taps. As phones become more powerful, some families no longer see a reason to own a separate computer.

Nevertheless, a small screen is not ideal for every task. Writing a long report, analysing a spreadsheet, editing a video or comparing several sources is usually easier with a full keyboard and a larger display. Relying only on phones may also create an educational gap: students can consume information easily but struggle to produce complex work. Instead of asking which device will completely replace the other, consumers should consider which tool is appropriate for each task and whether shared computers can provide affordable access.

context.source_line: Original mock local newspaper written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Why Weekenders Are Heading North
body: Short trips from Hong Kong to Shenzhen have become an attractive weekend choice. Faster cross-boundary transport allows visitors to reach shopping centres, restaurants, parks and entertainment venues without taking a flight. Many travellers also believe that food, personal services and family activities offer good value, so a day trip can feel like an affordable change from their normal routine.

Shenzhen’s appeal is not based on price alone. New districts, large indoor attractions and rapidly changing technology give repeat visitors something different to explore. Digital payment, online booking and recommendations shared on social media make planning easier. At the same time, crowded checkpoints, unfamiliar applications and differences in service expectations can create inconvenience for some travellers.

Hong Kong businesses cannot compete simply by asking residents to stay. They need to offer experiences worth choosing, such as neighbourhood events, creative packages, family discounts or late-night activities linked to local culture. Better service and clearer value may encourage residents to divide their leisure spending between both cities rather than treating the choice as a competition with only one winner.

context.source_line: Original mock news webpage written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Is Learning to Drive Worth It in Hong Kong?
body: For some Hong Kong residents, driving offers privacy, comfort and direct access to places that are difficult to reach by public transport. It can be especially useful for families with young children, elderly relatives or heavy equipment. Learning to drive may also provide a practical skill for travel or future employment, even if a person does not immediately buy a car.

The disadvantages are equally clear. Vehicles, fuel, insurance, tolls and parking are expensive, while traffic and limited parking spaces can turn a short journey into a stressful one. Hong Kong’s rail and bus networks already serve most urban areas, so many teenagers see little need to spend time and money on lessons before they can afford a vehicle.

Whether Hong Kong is car-friendly depends on whom the transport system is designed to serve. Policies that make driving easier may increase congestion and pollution, but policies that discourage cars can inconvenience people with genuine needs. Young people should therefore consider cost, safety, environmental impact and future usefulness before deciding whether a driving licence is an important step towards adulthood.

context.source_line: Original mock magazine written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Understanding the Fears Teenagers Carry
body: Teenage fears are not limited to obvious phobias such as heights, insects or enclosed spaces. Many students worry about examination results, disappointing their families, speaking in front of others or being rejected by friends. Online comparison can make these concerns feel more serious because young people repeatedly see carefully edited versions of other people’s success and appearance.

Fear can be useful when it warns someone about real danger, but it becomes harmful when it prevents normal learning, relationships or daily activities. Avoiding every uncomfortable situation may provide short-term relief while making the fear stronger. Adults sometimes dismiss teenage worries as unimportant, which can leave a young person feeling ashamed or unwilling to seek support.

Helpful responses depend on the seriousness of the problem. Talking to trusted friends, parents, teachers or counsellors can make a fear easier to understand. Gradual practice, reliable information and healthy routines may also build confidence. Schools should create a climate in which asking for help is treated as responsible behaviour, while serious or continuing anxiety receives professional attention.

context.source_line: Original mock local newspaper written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Wildlife Tourism: Protection or Performance?
body: Animal encounters are sold as unforgettable travel experiences. Visitors may watch dolphin shows, ride elephants or camels, photograph captive wild animals, or join tours that promise close contact with creatures in their natural habitat. Such activities can create jobs and fund conservation, especially where local communities have few other sources of income.

The same industry can also cause serious harm. Animals may be trained through fear, kept in unsuitable spaces or forced to interact with visitors for long hours. Even apparently harmless wildlife watching can disturb feeding and breeding when boats, vehicles or crowds move too close. Tourists often cannot tell whether an operator’s conservation claims are genuine.

Responsible tourism requires more than choosing an activity that looks educational. Travellers should examine how animals are housed, whether physical contact is necessary and where the money goes. Governments can set welfare standards and punish misleading operators, while communities can design smaller tours that protect habitats. A successful activity should improve the long-term well-being of both wildlife and local residents.

context.source_line: Original mock news website written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: From Bands to Solo Stars
body: Popular music once depended heavily on bands whose members developed a shared sound and public identity. Today, individual performers can record at home, collaborate remotely and reach listeners through short videos or streaming platforms. This makes it easier for solo artists to enter the market without waiting for a record company or several band members to agree on every decision.

Bands still offer something distinctive. Live instruments, different personalities and visible teamwork can create performances that one singer cannot easily reproduce. Groups may also divide the work of composing, arranging and interacting with fans. However, disagreements, higher touring costs and the difficulty of maintaining a stable line-up can make a band harder to manage.

Social media affects both types of performer. A memorable clip may introduce unknown musicians to millions of viewers, but algorithms can reward appearance and constant posting more than musical skill. Trends change quickly, and artists may feel pressure to produce short, attention-grabbing content. The future of pop music will depend on whether audiences continue to value strong songs and live performance alongside online popularity.

context.source_line: Original mock local magazine written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Self-Care Is More Than a Day Off
body: Self-care is often presented online as buying treats or escaping from responsibilities, but its basic purpose is to maintain physical and mental health. Enough sleep, regular movement, balanced meals, supportive relationships and time away from constant notifications can help students manage pressure. These habits are simple to describe but difficult to maintain during busy school terms.

A school Self-Care Month could introduce practical activities rather than one-off slogans. Short exercise sessions, sleep workshops, quiet spaces, peer-support training and guidance on seeking professional help could serve different needs. Activities should avoid suggesting that students are personally responsible for every problem when workload, family pressure or bullying may also affect well-being.

Participation is more likely when events are private, flexible and free from judgement. Student leaders can help choose relevant activities, but teachers and health professionals should provide reliable information. Success should not be measured only by attendance. The school should also ask whether students feel safer requesting help and whether healthy routines continue after the campaign ends.

context.title: More Than One Kind of School Movie
body: A school movie festival can introduce students to stories and styles they would not normally choose. Anime films such as Spirited Away combine detailed visual design with themes about courage, identity, family and the environment. Their popularity among young audiences may attract students who rarely attend school cultural events, while subtitles can make a Japanese-language film accessible.

A successful programme should still offer variety. Comedy, documentary, science fiction, local cinema and short student productions may appeal to different age groups and interests. Activities around the screenings can turn passive viewing into a shared experience. Students might join a costume display, animation workshop, film quiz, review competition or discussion with a local creator. The festival should balance entertainment with learning and provide alternatives for students who are not anime fans. Audience feedback can then guide the selection of future films.

context.source_line: Original mock online newspaper written in an HKDSE-style format; not an official HKEAA passage:
context.title: Can a Personality Test Choose Your Career?
body: Online personality tests have become popular among teenagers because they provide quick labels and attractive descriptions. Career advisers sometimes use structured questionnaires to help students discuss whether they prefer independent work, social interaction, careful routines or creative problem-solving. A result can give a student helpful vocabulary for describing strengths and possible working environments.

Problems arise when a test is treated as a final answer. People may respond differently depending on mood or experience, and broad categories cannot capture every ability, value or circumstance. A teenager may avoid an interesting subject because a result says it does not match one “type”. Employers may also use weak tests unfairly when judging applicants.

Career choices should combine several kinds of evidence. Students can speak to advisers, interview workers, try short courses, volunteer, complete internships and reflect on subjects they enjoy. Personality tests may begin a conversation, but they should not close it. The most useful plan allows interests and skills to change as a young person gains knowledge and real experience.

Its cultural value does not remove the need for strict safety. Weather, damaged materials, poor platforms or incorrect ties can endanger workers and people below. Public education may help people understand the craft without romanticising risk. The strongest approach would judge bamboo and metal systems by evidence, use each where appropriate and make worker protection the first requirement.

A flexible policy can improve access without making production demands impossible for a student team.

context.title: Personal Shopping in an Age of AI
body: A personal shopper helps clients choose products that suit their needs, budget or style. The job may involve researching items, visiting stores, arranging fittings and explaining alternatives. Teenagers with strong communication skills could gain useful experience through supervised part-time work, but they would also need reliability, product knowledge and respect for customer privacy.

Artificial intelligence can already recommend products from browsing history, answer routine questions and create virtual images of clothing. Such tools may make shopping faster, yet they can repeat biased data, encourage unnecessary purchases or misunderstand a client’s feelings. Shopping will probably combine digital and physical services rather than move entirely in one direction. Customers may research online, try items in a store and receive advice from both software and staff. Future personal shoppers will need to use technology without becoming controlled by it. context.title: Why Old Games Still Find New Players
body: Classic video games such as Super Mario Bros remain popular even though their graphics and controls are simpler than those of modern titles. Clear goals, memorable music and carefully designed challenges allow new players to understand them quickly. Older players may also return because the games are connected to childhood memories and can be shared across generations.

Video games have stayed popular by changing with technology. Online play, mobile devices, live streaming and independent developers have brought games to wider audiences. Future games may use more realistic virtual worlds, artificial intelligence and movement-based controls, but technical power will not guarantee enjoyment. Cost, privacy, excessive play and age suitability will remain important concerns. The most successful games are likely to combine new forms of interaction with the qualities that made classic games last: understandable rules, fair challenge and a reason to try again.

context.title: Teenagers Build Professional Profiles Online
body: LinkedIn and similar professional networks are attracting some teenagers who want to learn about careers, internships and university pathways. Unlike entertainment-focused platforms, a professional profile highlights skills, projects and achievements. Students may follow organisations, contact mentors and discover types of work that they had not previously considered.

Early networking can be useful, but it also creates pressure to present an impressive public identity before a young person has much experience. Profiles may exaggerate achievements, and job information shared online is not automatically reliable. Public contact details, messages from strangers and permanent records of careless posts create privacy and safety concerns.

Schools can teach students to check an organisation’s official website, compare claims across sources and ask a trusted adult before accepting an opportunity. A simple, truthful profile may help with exploration without forcing students to choose one career too early. Social media can open a door, but real preparation still requires study, practical experience, reflection and conversations with people who understand the work.

part_a.instruction: Your Careers Team is preparing a feature on the growing popularity of LinkedIn among teenagers and the role of social media in career planning. Discuss the following points.

discussion_points.text: Why are more teenagers choosing LinkedIn over other social media platforms
Can social media play a positive role in helping people build and grow their careers
Should secondary school students begin thinking seriously about their future career paths
anything else you think is important

part_b.instruction: The examiner will ask you one or more questions based on Part A. You will have up to 1 minute to respond.

questions.text: What are some common ways teenagers explore and prepare for future job opportunities?
Do you think sharing your profile on social media can help with job searching?
What can be done to check if the information on social media is trustworthy?
How do you think social media helps people discover career opportunities?
Do you personally use any social media platforms?
What kind of job are you hoping to have in the future?
What types of jobs do you think teenagers are most likely to pursue in the coming years?
Which social media platforms do you think are the most popular right now?
